subject: Vocabulary
topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers
description: Itinerary, sojourn, expedition, peripatetic, transit, exodus, voyage, embark

questions.stem: An ITINERARY is best described as:

options.option_text: A vehicle used for tourist travel
A planned route or schedule of a journey
A travel diary written after the trip
A passport stamp issued at the border

questions.explanation: ITINERARY — Latin 'iter' (journey). A planned route + schedule of stops, dates, activities. 'Detailed itinerary for the 7-day trip.' Distractor 1 = vehicle. Distractor 3 = travelogue. Distractor 4 = visa stamp.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

options.option_text: A short trip to a nearby destination quickly
A temporary stay at a place during a journey
A permanent residence in a foreign country
A solo backpacking trip across a continent

questions.explanation: SOJOURN — French origin; a TEMPORARY stay. Implies the traveller will move on. 'A brief sojourn in Paris before flying to Rome.' Synonyms: stopover, layover, visit. Distractor 1 = excursion. Distractor 3 = settlement / immigration. Distractor 4 = backpacking trip.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

options.option_text: A short trip to a local market or shop
An organised journey for exploration or research
A casual weekend visit to relatives' homes
A daily commute to work and back home

questions.explanation: EXPEDITION — Latin 'expedire' (to set free, prepare for action). An ORGANISED journey with a specific purpose: exploration, research, scientific study, military operation. Examples: Antarctic expedition, Mount Everest expedition, Magellan's circumnavigation, Lewis & Clark expedition. Distractors describe routine / casual travel.

questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A PERIPATETIC person is one who:

options.option_text: Is afraid of any travel beyond home
Travels frequently from place to place
Lives only in one place all life
Refuses to walk and prefers vehicles

questions.explanation: PERIPATETIC — Greek 'peripatetikos' (walking around). Wandering, frequent traveller, itinerant. 'Aristotle's peripatetic school' — he taught while walking. Modern usage: 'A peripatetic teacher who works at multiple schools.' Distractor 1 = agoraphobic / hodophobic. Distractor 3 = sedentary. Distractor 4 unrelated.

questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

questions.stem: An EXODUS is most accurately defined as:

options.option_text: A small group's casual short trip
A mass departure of people from a place
A circular movement returning to start
A solo adventurer's brief detour

questions.explanation: EXODUS — Greek 'ex-' (out) + 'hodos' (way). MASS DEPARTURE / migration. Famous example: Biblical Exodus (Israelites' departure from Egypt). Modern usage: 'Mass exodus from cities during the COVID-19 lockdown.' Antonym: INFLUX. Synonym: emigration (when crossing borders). Distractors describe other small-scale movements.

questions.stem: To EMBARK on a journey means to:

options.option_text: End or complete a journey successfully
Begin or start a journey, especially by ship
Cancel a journey midway through it
Pause a journey for a brief rest stop

questions.explanation: EMBARK — Old French 'embarquer' (board a ship). Originally a nautical term: to board a ship. By extension: to BEGIN a journey or undertaking. 'They embarked on a new business venture.' Antonym: DISEMBARK (to get off, especially a ship). Distractor 1 = arrive / disembark. Distractors 3, 4 are unrelated.

questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A NOMAD is best described as:

options.option_text: A person living permanently in one city
A person who moves from place to place seasonally
A person travelling only for sightseeing tours
A scientist studying ancient migration patterns

questions.explanation: NOMAD — Greek 'nomas' (roaming for pasture). Member of a community or culture that MOVES SEASONALLY rather than settles permanently — usually following pasture, water, or herds. Examples: Bedouins (Arabian desert), Mongolian herders, Maasai (East Africa), Banjaras (India), Roma. Modern 'digital nomad' — remote workers travelling continuously. Antonym: SETTLED. Distractors are not nomadic in this sense.

questions.topic: Travel and motion words — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a WAYFARER?

options.option_text: A traveller who journeys from place to place on foot
A professional guide hired to lead organised trekking tours
A sailor who navigates long sea voyages using star charts
A merchant who travels between towns to barter or sell goods

questions.explanation: A wayfarer is a traveller, especially one who journeys on foot. The word derives from Old English 'weg' (road) + 'faran' (to travel). Options B, C, and D describe travellers with specific occupational roles, whereas wayfarer is a general term for any foot-traveller making a journey.

questions.stem: When a traveller is described as being IN TRANSIT, it means they are?

options.option_text: resting at a midpoint to recover energy for the next leg
passing through a location briefly en route to their final stop
changing their mode of transport from land to air or sea
waiting for official clearance to legally enter a foreign country

questions.explanation: Transit comes from Latin 'transire' meaning to go across or pass through. Being in transit means passing through a place on the way to a final destination. Option C is the most tempting distractor because airport transit lounges are associated with changing flights, but transit itself means the passage through a place, not the act of switching transport.

questions.stem: PEREGRINATION most closely refers to which type of journey?

options.option_text: a swift, direct journey undertaken for urgent official duties
a long, wandering journey passing through many different places
a circular route specifically designed to return to the starting point
a covert journey undertaken to escape pursuit or detection

questions.explanation: Peregrination derives from Latin 'peregrinari' (to travel abroad or through foreign lands) and denotes an extended, often meandering journey through multiple places. Option A describes a mission or errand; Option C describes a circuit or round trip; Option D describes a fugitive's flight — none of these capture the wandering, unhurried quality of a peregrination.

questions.stem: The verb MEANDER, when applied to a traveller's path, implies?

options.option_text: moving in a slow, winding course without a fixed destination
travelling at a brisk, steady pace to maximise distance covered
retracing one's steps repeatedly due to navigational errors
following a strict pre-planned route with precisely timed stops

questions.explanation: Meander derives from the ancient River Maeander (modern Büyük Menderes, Turkey), famous for its winding, sinuous course. Applied to travellers it means following an aimless, winding path. Option C (retracing steps) confuses meandering with backtracking — meandering moves forward but not in a straight line, not backward.

questions.stem: To PERAMBULATE an area, as used in formal or literary English, most accurately means to?

options.option_text: walk through or around it in a leisurely, unhurried manner
survey its terrain using specialised geographical instruments
travel through it at speed, covering as much ground as possible
establish a temporary base camp within it for extended fieldwork

questions.explanation: Perambulate comes from Latin 'per' (through) + 'ambulare' (to walk), meaning to walk through or around an area, typically at a leisurely pace. Option B describes surveying, not walking; Option C contradicts the unhurried connotation; Option D describes camping, not movement. The word perambulator (pram) for a baby carriage derives from the same root.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly distinguishes MEANDER from GALLIVANT as travel-related verbs?

options.option_text: Meander implies aimless wandering; gallivant implies carefree pleasure travel
Meander implies swift motion; gallivant implies slow, reluctant movement
Meander applies only to waterways; gallivant applies only to land journeys
Meander implies purposeful travel; gallivant implies involuntary displacement

questions.explanation: Meander implies a winding, aimless course (the movement is the defining feature), while gallivant specifically implies light-hearted, pleasure-seeking roaming. Option C is the most tempting distractor because meander etymologically came from a river's name, but in modern English it freely describes any winding path or movement — it is not restricted to water contexts.

questions.stem: The word TRAIPSE, in travel contexts, carries which connotation that is absent from the neutral verb WALK?

options.option_text: walking wearily or reluctantly, often across tiresome or unpleasant terrain
walking with measured, athletic precision on technically difficult ground
walking quietly and carefully so as not to disturb others nearby
walking swiftly with confident strides directly toward a known landmark

questions.explanation: Traipse carries a strong connotation of weariness, tedium, or reluctance — one traipses when compelled to walk somewhere inconvenient or exhausting (e.g. 'traipsing through muddy fields'). Option D (swift, confident strides) is the near-opposite. Option B (athletic precision) describes trekking or scrambling. Traipse never implies skill, speed, or willingness, which makes it semantically distinct from walk, hike, or stride.
